property|model:114340500867371532|UnityEditor.VFX.VFXUI|stickyNoteInfos.Array.data[1].contents|String|To sample a mesh or a skinned mesh surface, we usually need “coordinates”: a triangle index and XY coordinates to know where to spawn on the desired triangle.

We want our particles to stick to the skinned mesh surface, and those coordinates' information will be needed at different stages of the simulation. 

We're creating the needed coordinates and storing them in a custom Vector3 attribute.

property|model:114340500867371532|UnityEditor.VFX.VFXUI|stickyNoteInfos.Array.data[2].contents|String|We're using the “set position on skinned mesh” block.
We're inputting a skinned mesh property to be able to reference a skinned mesh from the scene. 

To know where to spawn on the mesh, we're using the previously created coordinates.

property|model:114340500867371532|UnityEditor.VFX.VFXUI|stickyNoteInfos.Array.data[3].contents|String|We're using the current particle position to sample Perlin noise. This noise is used to drive the color and size of our particles.


Using noise instead of random numbers to drive particle attributes like color and size can give interesting results.
This can lead to spatially coherent values, which often look more organic and natural than pure random.

property|model:114340500867371532|UnityEditor.VFX.VFXUI|stickyNoteInfos.Array.data[4].contents|String|We're using the previously stored coordinates to sample the skinned mesh with the sample skinned mesh operator. 

This allows us to get the UV coordinates. With the UV from the skinned mesh, we can sample its textures.
The alpha channel of its texture is then used to kill particles with an alpha value lower than 0.1.
This method is usually called “rejection sampling.”

property|model:114340500867371532|UnityEditor.VFX.VFXUI|stickyNoteInfos.Array.data[5].contents|String|The “set position” block is getting the direction from the skinned mesh normals.
We want to use those normals to orient our feathers.
To give some fake bouncy motion, we're adding noise to the direction attribute.

property|model:114340500867371532|UnityEditor.VFX.VFXUI|stickyNoteInfos.Array.data[6].contents|String|We're randomizing the blend value between the correct skinned mesh normal computed by the block and the previously noised direction value.

This adds some fake secondary motion to give more life to the feathers, so they don't look too static or stiff.

property|model:114340500867371532|UnityEditor.VFX.VFXUI|stickyNoteInfos.Array.data[7].contents|String|By using a “set position skinned mesh” block in the Update Context, we're able to make our particles stick to the geometry.

As we're using from frame to frame the same coordinates that we stored previously in the initialize context, we can be sure that each particle will sample the same triangle from frame to frame.

If you enter play mode, you should see the creature moving and the feather sticking to its surface.
